unit-m4u1.title: Unit 4 · Lesson 1: Multiply Decimals by Powers of 10
unit-m4u1.source: enVision Topic 4 Student Edition practice pages — multiplying decimals (Drive)

summary.text: Lesson 4-1 practice pages: using place-value patterns to multiply decimals by 10, 100, 1,000 and by powers of 10 written with exponents, finding a missing exponent, and word problems about magnified sizes.

why.text: Multiplying by powers of 10 is the pattern the rest of the unit leans on: placing the decimal point in every later product uses the same idea.

objectives.text: Read powers of 10 written with exponents
Find a missing exponent from where the decimal point moved
Explain why 3.8 and 3.80 are the same number

parentNote.text: Built from the lesson 4-1 practice pages in her Unit 4 folder, read for what they ask. The numbers are fresh, not the page's own. Every wrong option on a worked product comes from a named slip: moving the point the wrong way, one place too few or too many, or reading 10³ as "10 times 3". The last one is the slip most worth a word, because 7.3 × 30 gives a believable number. Her class teaches this unit after Unit 5.

nextUp.text: Count the zeros, move the point that many places right, then check that the number grew.

cards.def:
**A power of 10 is 10 multiplied by itself: 10¹ = 10, 10² = 100, 10³ = 1,000.**
• The small raised number, the exponent, counts the 10s.
• It also equals the number of zeros.

**Multiplying by a power of 10 moves the decimal point to the right, one place for each zero.**
• 2.57 × 100 = 257 (2 places).
• 0.064 × 1,000 = 64 (3 places).

**Really the digits move: each one shifts one place left and is worth 10 times as much.**
• In 4.2 the 4 is ones; in 42 the 4 is tens.

**When the point runs past the last digit, write zeros to fill the empty places.**
• 13.8 × 10⁴ = 138,000.

cards.term: The exponent is not a factor
cards.hint: Count the tens; do not multiply by the little number.

cards.term: Zeros at the end of a decimal
cards.def:
**A zero after the last digit to the right of the point does not change the value.**
• 3.8 = 3.80 = 3.800.

**Count how many places the point moved; that is the exponent.**
• 0.48 → 480 moves 3 places, so it is × 10³.

**Multiplying by a power of 10 always makes a number bigger, so check that your answer grew.**
• To undo it, divide, and the point moves left.
• A microscope that shows 2.5 cm at × 100 means the real thing is 0.025 cm.

questions.q: When you multiply a decimal by 10³, which way does the decimal point move, and how far?
opts: It stays put, and you write three zeros on the end
questions.hint: Multiplying by a power of 10 makes a number bigger. Count the zeros in 1,000.
steps: 10³ = 1,000, which has 3 zeros.
Each 10 moves the point one place.
Bigger means the digits move left, so the point moves right.
So the point moves 3 places to the right.

ex.main: **3 places to the right.** 10³ is 1,000, which has 3 zeros. Writing zeros after the last digit, 2.5 → 2.5000, changes nothing.
ex.tip: Count the exponent or the zeros: that is how many places.

questions.hint: The small 2 says how many 10s are multiplied together.
steps: The small raised number is the exponent.
It says how many 10s are multiplied.

ex.main: **10 × 10, which is 100.** The exponent counts the 10s; it is not a number to multiply by.
ex.tip: The exponent is a count of tens.

questions.q: Mira's ribbon is 3.8 meters long. Theo's ribbon is 3.80 meters long. Whose ribbon is longer?
opts: Mira's, because 3.8 has fewer digits to read
Neither: 3.8 and 3.80 are the same length
You cannot tell from these two numbers
questions.hint: What is in the hundredths place of 3.8?
steps: 3.8 has 8 tenths and 0 hundredths.
3.80 has 8 tenths and 0 hundredths too.
A zero at the end, after the decimal point, does not change the value.
So the ribbons are the same length.

ex.main: **Neither: they are the same length.** 3.80 just writes the 0 hundredths that 3.8 leaves out.
ex.tip: Zeros at the end of a decimal do not change its value.

questions.q: When a number is multiplied by 10, what happens to each digit?
opts: It stays in its place, and a zero joins the end
It moves one place to the right and is worth less
It stays in its place and is worth 10 more
It moves one place to the left and is worth 10 times as much
questions.hint: Think of 4.2 × 10 = 42. Where did the 4 go?
steps: In 4.2 the 4 is in the ones place.
In 42 the 4 is in the tens place.
It moved one place left, so it is worth 10 times as much.

ex.main: **Each digit moves one place left and is worth 10 times as much.** That is why the point seems to move right.
ex.tip: The digits move; the point is just where it was.

questions.hint: How many places did the point move to go from 0.48 to 480?
steps: 0.48 → 4.8 is one place.
4.8 → 48 is two places.
48 → 480 is three places.
So the power is 3: 0.48 × 10³ = 480.

ex.main: **3.** The point moves 3 places, so it is 10 × 10 × 10 = 10³. 2 stops at 48, 4 goes on to 4,800, and 1 stops at 4.8.
ex.tip: Count the moves, one place at a time.

steps: 10² = 100, so the decimal point moves 2 places to the right.
Move it one place at a time: 2.57 → 25.7 → 257.
Multiplying by 100 makes a number bigger, so 257 makes sense.

ex.main: **257.** 100 has 2 zeros, so the point moves 2 places right. The wrong answers come from real slips: 0.0257 is the point moved the wrong way, to the left; 25.7 is the point moved one place too few; 2,570 is the point moved one place too many.
ex.tip: Bigger, so the point moves right.

questions.hint: The point moves 3 places. The zero in front stops mattering.
steps: 10³ = 1,000, so the decimal point moves 3 places to the right.
Move it one place at a time: 0.064 → 0.64 → 6.4 → 64.
Multiplying by 1,000 makes a number bigger, so 64 makes sense.

ex.main: **64.** 1,000 has 3 zeros, so the point moves 3 places right. The wrong answers come from real slips: 0.000064 is the point moved the wrong way, to the left; 6.4 is the point moved one place too few; 640 is the point moved one place too many.
ex.tip: Leading zeros fall away as the number grows.

questions.hint: Move the point 4 places. You will need to write zeros to fill the places.
steps: 10⁴ = 10,000, so the decimal point moves 4 places to the right.
Move it one place at a time: 13.8 → 138 → 1,380 → 13,800 → 138,000.
Multiplying by 10,000 makes a number bigger, so 138,000 makes sense.

ex.main: **138,000.** 10,000 has 4 zeros, so the point moves 4 places right. The wrong answers come from real slips: 0.00138 is the point moved the wrong way, to the left; 13,800 is the point moved one place too few; 1,380,000 is the point moved one place too many.
ex.tip: Fill empty places with zeros as you move.

steps: 10³ = 1,000, so the decimal point moves 3 places to the right.
Move it one place at a time: 7.3 → 73 → 730 → 7,300.
Multiplying by 1,000 makes a number bigger, so 7,300 makes sense.

ex.main: **7,300.** 1,000 has 3 zeros, so the point moves 3 places right. The wrong answers come from real slips: 0.0073 is the point moved the wrong way, to the left; 730 is the point moved one place too few; 219 is the exponent read as "times 3", so 10³ became 30.
ex.tip: The exponent counts places; it is not a factor.

questions.hint: Watch the zero inside 0.705. It stays where it is.
steps: 10² = 100, so the decimal point moves 2 places to the right.
Move it one place at a time: 0.705 → 7.05 → 70.5.
Multiplying by 100 makes a number bigger, so 70.5 makes sense.

ex.main: **70.5.** 100 has 2 zeros, so the point moves 2 places right. The wrong answers come from real slips: 0.00705 is the point moved the wrong way, to the left; 7.05 is the point moved one place too few; 705 is the point moved one place too many.
ex.tip: A zero between digits never disappears.

steps: 5.06 → 50.6 is one place.
50.6 → 506 is two places.
506 → 5,060 is three places.

ex.main: **3.** Three moves of the point. 2 stops at 506, 4 goes on to 50,600, and 1 stops at 50.6.

questions.q: A magnifying lens makes things look 10 times their actual size. A ladybug is 0.6 cm long. How long does it look through the lens?
steps: The lens multiplies the size by 10.
0.6 × 10: the point moves one place right.
So it looks 6 cm long.

ex.main: **6 cm.** 0.6 × 10 = 6. 0.06 moves the point the wrong way, 60 moves it two places, and 10.6 adds 10 instead of multiplying.
ex.tip: "10 times" means multiply by 10, never add 10.

questions.q: A microscope shows things at 100 times their actual size. Seen through it, a grain of pollen is 2.5 cm across. How big is it really?
questions.hint: The microscope multiplied by 100. To undo that, do the opposite.
steps: Seen size = actual size × 100.
So actual size = seen size ÷ 100.
Dividing by 100 moves the point 2 places left: 2.5 → 0.25 → 0.025.
So the pollen is 0.025 cm across.

ex.main: **0.025 cm.** The microscope multiplied by 100, so divide by 100 to undo it. 250 multiplies a second time, and 0.25 and 25 move the point the wrong number of places.
ex.tip: Real things under a microscope are tiny. A huge answer is a sign you multiplied.

questions.hint: Check each one by counting how many places the point should move.
steps: 6.15 × 100: 2 places right is 615. True.

ex.main: **6.15 × 100 = 615.** Each of the others moves the point one place too many or one too few.
ex.tip: Count the zeros, then count the moves.

questions.q: A rope is 4.5 meters long. A second rope is 10 times as long. How much longer is the second rope than the first?
questions.hint: First find the second rope's length. Then compare.
steps: The second rope is 4.5 × 10 = 45 meters.
How much longer means subtract.
So it is 40.5 meters longer.

ex.main: **40.5 meters.** 4.5 × 10 = 45, and 45 − 4.5 = 40.5. 45 is the rope's length, not the difference, and 49.5 adds instead of subtracting.
